claims.text: The initial HfNbTiVAl10 material is arc-melted.
HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchically heterogeneous microstructure containing multiscale grains and phase distributions.
The initial HfNbTiVAl10 material is in a homogenized condition.
A supervised machine-learning model using phase fractions, grain size, and defect features can predict tensile and fracture properties of HfNbTiVAl10.
Hierarchical phase arrangement and grain-size gradients are key predictive inputs for HfNbTiVAl10.
Hierarchical phase arrangement and grain-size gradients govern dislocation motion in HfNbTiVAl10.
Hierarchical phase arrangement and grain-size gradients govern crack initiation and propagation in HfNbTiVAl10.
Data-driven modeling can capture complex dependencies between alloy descriptors and mechanical response.
A model using hierarchical microstructure descriptors captures HfNbTiVAl10 mechanical response more effectively than classical continuum or simplified constitutive models.
The machine-learning approach will reduce Young's-modulus prediction error by about 20% relative to conventional simulations.
The machine-learning approach will reduce yield-strength prediction error by about 20% relative to conventional simulations.
The machine-learning approach will reduce fracture-toughness prediction error by about 20% relative to conventional simulations.
The machine-learning approach will decrease computational or evaluation time by about 30% relative to conventional simulations.
Continuum-based or classical phenomenological models are the established baseline for predicting hierarchical high-entropy-alloy behavior under tensile and fracture loading.
Model performance may degrade when applied outside the microstructural or processing range represented in its training data.
Large composition changes or extreme thermomechanical treatments may place specimens outside the model's reliable domain.
The expected accuracy and efficiency gains depend on the fidelity and completeness of the training dataset.

contradictions.description: The boundary explicitly permits degradation outside the training microstructure/process range, but the falsification experiment deliberately creates previously unobserved microstructures outside the original training range and treats poor predictions there as invalidating the hypothesis.
